📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Val Chmerkovskiy and Jenna Johnson may not be adding another Mirrorball to their household, but they're still having a ball at home.

A day after Johnson and her partner Harry Shum Jr. were voted off Dancing With the Stars following his and his partner Jenna Dewan’s elimination the week prior, Chmerkovskiy demonstrated his support for his wife with a steamy comment.

Industry observers note that “Keep the trophy’s [sic],” the 40-year-old shared on his Instagram Stories Nov. 18 alongside a photo of Johnson from a red carpet event. “I get to watch this baddie brush her teeth naked every morning.” Chmerkovskiy—who shares son Rome, 3, with his wife of seven years—also thirsted after her by adding a drool emoji.

It has been revealed that johnson and Shum were shockingly sent home on the Nov. 17 semifinals after receiving perfect scores 30 out of 30 for both of their dances: a paso doble to Rihanna's "We Found Love” and a quickstep to Amy Winehouse's “Valerie,” in which Shum paid tribute to late Glee costar Naya Rivera.

While some believe viewers made a major misstep by sending the pair home, the duo slammed the negativity they mentioned they received online, sharing they think it impacted their relationship with the rest of the season 35 cast.

“I hope to get to know them more,” Shum told E! News in an interview following their elimination Nov. 17, “because it's just been so chaotic.”.

“We're a bit all trauma bonded,” Johnson chimed in, to which Shum added, “There's a lot of trauma bond just because this year has been a little crazy.”.

According to recent reports, “Social media is a little nuts,” he continued. “I hope they address that at a certain point, because I think there's a good amount of bullying that doesn't feel really good, and I think the rest of the cast feels it.”.

Though Shum didn’t go into specifics, he and Johnson were spun into drama after Chmerkovskiy received a one-week suspension from the show following his now-infamous reaction to a critique judge Carrie Ann Inaba made after one of Johnson and Shum’s performances, in which he referenced Will Smith’s 2022 Oscar slap.

Shum seemingly referred to the fallout as he praised Johnson after they were voted off.

In a recent development, “I want to say you have been dealing with everything with grace, with the noise outside,” the Grey’s Anatomy star told his partner on air, “and teaching me the things that I have only dreamed of to learn, and this has been one of the most beautiful experiences. So, thank you so much.”.

As DWTS prepares to tango into its season 35 finale, read on for a deep dive into the secrets of the ballroom….

How Much Do the Celebrities Get Paid to Be on Dancing With the Stars?

Recent findings suggest that citing multiple sources, Variety reported in 2019 that Dancing With the Stars contestants make $125,000 for the rehearsal period and first two weeks of the show. If they progress beyond that point, the outlet continued, they earn more money each week. At the time, sources told the publication stars could earn a maximum of $295,000.

However, Bobby Bones said he made more than this when he won season 27 with Sharna Burgess in 2018.

Recent findings suggest that "That show pays OK," the radio personality said on a Sept. 2025 episode of Jason Tartick's podcast Trading Secrets. "Like, first episode, no money. Second episode, $10,000. I think it's like, $10,000, $10,000, $20,000, $20,000. It ends up being $50,000 an episode if you last.".

Also receiving a base salary of around $110,000, Bones continued, "I ended up making close to $400,000 from that show.".

ABC has not publicly confirmed any of these figures.

What Do the Pros Get Paid on Dancing With the Stars?

Similarly, little has been shared publicly about how much the pros get paid. But as with the contestants, it seems like the longer they're on the show, the more money they can make.

But even if a pro is eliminated in the first round, they're not leaving the ballroom empty-handed.

"You're guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks," Jenna Johnson said on a June 2025 episode of Kelly Stafford and Hank Winchester's podcast The Morning After. "I think there's different contracts though. I can't speak for everybody.".

Do Pros Get Paid More If They Win Dancing With the Stars?

While Johnson—who won season 26 with Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon, as well as season 33 with The Bachelor's Joey Graziadei—says the pros don't get a larger paycheck if they take home what is now called the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, she noted there's still an incentive to make it to the finale (besides bragging rights, of course).

"If you make it all the way to the end, you're getting paid the whole season, which is amazing, and you get a bonus on top of that for making it to the finale," she explained on The Morning After. "If you win, it's not like you win a $1 million and split it with your partner. You're just getting a cute trophy together.".

Do the Troupe Members Get Paid as Much as the Pros on Dancing With the Stars?

That doesn't appear to be the case.

On a 2022 episode of Trading Secrets, Lindsay Arnold recalled how her salary was cut "more than in half" when she was demoted from pro to troupe member.

How Are Pros and Celebrities Paired Together on Dancing With the Stars?

The pros get little input when it comes to being matched with a celebrity.

"You get no say," Lindsay noted on a May 2025 episode of Maggie Sellers' Hot Smart Rich podcast. "It's very much just, 'Here's your partner. Make it work.'".

In fact, Jenna said the pairing is often a secret until the last minute.

"They really want to keep it a secret until you meet them live," Jenna remarked on The Morning After. "They want that genuine reaction. So I think people always think we know who we have and we're keeping it a secret. Absolutely not. They do not tell us. They really don't even want us to know the cast. It gets leaked a lot, but they want it very hush-hush until you walk in and meet your partner.".

As for what the Dancing With the Stars team looks for when making these matches?

Recent findings suggest that "It's based on height, build and personality and compatibility," former showrunner Rob Wade told E! News in 2015. "We don't pair people who aren't going to get on. It's too intense. It's not like The Bachelor or something, we couldn't do that. That would just be miserable experience for the celebrity, for us and the viewer. You don't want to see two people who don't like each other and, quite frankly, we have made that mistake pairing people up who didn't get on so well.".

How Often Do the Pros and Celebrities Practice on Dancing With the Stars?

Recent findings suggest that put simply, a lot."Every day we have four-hour rehearsals," Rylee Arnold, who was partnered with Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik on season 33, shared on a September 2024 episode of the Lightweights Podcast With Joe Vulpis. "It’s either 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. or 5:00 p.m to 9:00 p.m."But the work doesn't stop once the rehearsal wraps. Rylee noted she might then meet with producers or the creative team, work on choreography or study dance videos."Literally my whole life is devoted to it," she continued, "but it's my passion and it's what I love. So, it makes me so happy."Indeed, it's a no-days-off kind of gig."We have our show day on Tuesday and then it's Wednesday to Sunday, straight rehearsals," Rylee added. "And then Monday we have camera blocking and then Tuesday's show day again.".

Do the Pros Get to Pick the Songs Each Week for Their Dance With Their Celebrity Partner?

"Mostly yes," Emma Slater and Britt Stewart revealed in a September 2025 Instagram video, "though it's a collaboration with producers.".

What's the Process Like for Making the Costumes for Dancing With the Stars?

If you thought the quickstep was fast, just wait until you hear about the pace of the costume department."We meet with the set and lighting designers, dancers and talent and create a story [for each pair]," costume designer Daniela Gschwendtner told TV Insider back in 2017. "Then we sketch out ideas. We have five days, max, to make all the outfits. That’s half a day per costume, not including all the rhinestones. The fitting and trimming we do later. We have about 20 people in our department and then we have a separate tailor shop. It’s a substantial enterprise."In fact, costume designer Steven Norman Lee noted pairs usually try on their costumes for the first time just hours before showtime. And while the department "might use a pair of pants again for the boys," he continued, everything is generally made custom each week.As Gschwendtner added, "We do reuse things for group numbers or promo shoots, but not for the competition. We don’t reuse things unless there’s a specific reason to do so. We try to keep everybody fresh and upcoming in something different every week, so it stays interesting.".

#610. Industry News: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

Industry News: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1485 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences.
  • It has been revealed that the team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information.
  • Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

It has been revealed that the team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

In a recent development, "Building a model in the abstract is one thing," stated Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab.".

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes.

For decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

Recent findings suggest that visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back.".

The new findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man.

Recent findings suggest that an important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

Industry observers note that at Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

Recent findings suggest that when researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

Recent findings suggest that producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

In a recent development, to address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise.

When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The upcoming approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

Recent findings suggest that another key discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

In a recent development, "Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler said. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation.".

The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person.

In a recent development, A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

Recent findings suggest that the participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

It has been revealed that the AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring people to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

Sources indicate that "A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler said. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around.".

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight.

According to recent reports, the research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration.".

Sources indicate that the project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

In a recent development, rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany.
  • This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?
  • Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany. For the 2029 federal election, it has set itself an ambitious goal: to see its co-chair Alice Weidel to become Germany's next chancellor.

This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?

Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.

"Viewed as a whole, the AfD is an extreme right-wing party that also displays tendencies associated with a fascist movement," mentioned Fabian Virchow, a researcher on right-wing extremism at Düsseldorf University of Applied Sciences, in an interview with DW.

Virchow identifies different factions and strategic tendencies within the party, some of which are at odds with one another. Party leader Alice Weidel, for example, is generally seen as a proponent of a free-market approach that seeks to keep the state as small as possible. Others, by contrast, favor a strong state shaped by an ethnically homogeneous people, among them Björn Höcke, the influential far-right AfD leader in the state of Thuringia.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that virchow sees a "normalization" of right-wing extremist positions within the AfD. In his view, this has made the party more attractive to neo-Nazi circles: "Today, many people see greater room for ethnonationalist and radical right-wing ideas.".

Support for this observation comes from the latest findings of the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study, one of the most widely cited long-term studies tracking right-wing extremist attitudes in Germany. The researchers behind the study have identified a rise in right-wing extremist views within German society, including a growing acceptance of ideologies rooted in the tradition of National Socialism.

Recent findings suggest that particularly striking is the finding that around two-thirds of people with firmly entrenched far-right worldviews would vote for the AfD. According to the study, the AfD has achieved what earlier far-right parties in Germany never managed: "to unite large segments of the electorate with anti-democratic attitudes behind it.".

Recent findings suggest that the debate has been further fueled by several recent incidents within the party. In 2026 alone, numerous AfD politicians and staff members made headlines over alleged ties to neo-Nazi organizations:.

Industry observers note that in August 2026, police carried out a large-scale raid targeting fifteen people. Authorities suspect them of continuing the activities of the so-called "Artgemeinschaft." Before it was banned in 2023, the group was considered one of Germany's largest and most influential neo-Nazi cadre organizations. Particularly explosive was the fact that two of those targeted in the raid are sitting AfD members of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. Their attorneys deny the allegations.

According to reporting by the German daily, Welt, four staff members of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt are former members of the now-banned "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" (HDJ), a neo-Nazi youth organization rooted in National Socialist racial ideology that organized paramilitary camps for young people. Two of the staff members held leadership positions within the HDJ and now work closely with AfD politician Ulrich Siegmund, who is seeking to become the AfD's first state premier in December.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Remarkably, both organizations, the "Artgemeinschaft" and the HDJ, are on the AfD's so-called incompatibility list, which is intended to draw a line between the party and extremist organizations and movements. In principle, anyone with a history of membership in such groups is supposed to be excluded from the party.

It has been revealed that but the list appears to be little more than a dead letter. In 2020, former AfD federal executive board member Andreas Kalbitz was expelled from the party after failing to disclose his membership in the "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" on his application to join. Yet according to the news magazine Spiegel, he is once again working for the AfD, this time as a staffer for Saxony-Anhalt state legislator Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, who has since become deputy speaker of the state parliament.

Industry observers note that the question of the AfD's relationship to National Socialism has dogged the party since its founding in 2013. Even in its early years, co-founder and first party leader Bernd Lucke sparked controversy when he described democracy and parliamentary politics in Germany as "degenerate," a term the Nazis used to disparage art and culture that did not conform to their ideological worldview.

In Germany, references to the Nazi dictatorship (1933-1945) under Adolf Hitler remain politically taboo because of the country's responsibility for World War Two and the Holocaust, the systematic mass murder of Europe's Jews.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

If AfD members or their staff have come under scrutiny because of past involvement in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations, they have generally sought to distance themselves from those backgrounds or from the ideologies associated with them.

Sources indicate that but how credible are these attempts at distancing? Laura Neumann* has worked with many people seeking to leave the far-right scene. She works for "Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts," a network of organizations that supports far-right cadres and activists as they disengage from the movement. "A successful exit is the result of a professionally guided process," she noted in an interview with DW.

Neumann describes leaving the far-right scene as a challenging process of self-confrontation. "When it comes to someone leaving the movement, the first question I always ask is: How does that person talk about their past? Have they genuinely come to terms with it?".

Based on the experience of exit counselors, one principle generally holds true: the longer and more deeply a person has been immersed in far-right circles, the more difficult it becomes to distance themselves from those beliefs and affiliations.

In a recent development, DW requested a statement from the AfD's federal executive board regarding its handling of party members who were previously active in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations. Individual lawmakers and parliamentary staff members were also asked to comment. None responded.

It has been revealed that the party's and its politicians' silence in the face of such allegations reflects an observation made by political scientist Fabian Virchow: "Within the AfD, there is no longer a perceived need to distance oneself from radical far-right positions. That is part of this process of normalization.".

Virchow indicates that right-wing extremism appears to have advanced so far into the mainstream of German society that efforts to scandalize it now remain largely ineffective.

Industry observers note that * Editor's note: To protect the privacy of the staff member of Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts, we have changed her name to Laura Neumann. Her real name is known to the editors.

This article was originally written in German.

#605. Industry News: A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2365 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2365 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A butterfly commonly seen throughout Central and South America has been concealing a remarkable secret.
  • The newly identified species, named Colobura cryptica, was described in the journal Zootaxa by researchers led by Anisha Sapkota, a doctoral student at the Florida Museum of Natural History.
  • Even more surprising, the three species occupy overlapping regions and can be found in the same places at the same time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A butterfly commonly seen throughout Central and South America has been concealing a remarkable secret. For more than two centuries, scientists believed that the genus Colobura contained just one widespread species. Now, researchers have identified a third species that looks almost identical to its relatives, raising upcoming questions about how these butterflies evolved and continue to live alongside one another.

The newly identified species, named Colobura cryptica, was described in the journal Zootaxa by researchers led by Anisha Sapkota, a doctoral student at the Florida Museum of Natural History. By combining DNA analysis with subtle differences in wing patterns and ultraviolet light reflection, the team uncovered distinctions that had remained largely invisible to scientists.

Even more surprising, the three species occupy overlapping regions and can be found in the same places at the same time. Yet genetic evidence suggests they remain separate, with no detectable signs of interbreeding.

A Familiar Butterfly With a Hidden Identity.

Recent findings suggest that central and South America's tropical rainforests contain some of the greatest concentrations of biodiversity on the planet. Costa Rica alone supports approximately half a million species, roughly five times the number found across Canada, even though Canada's land area is about 200 times larger.

Despite this extraordinary diversity, certain plants and animals are especially recognizable throughout the region. In Canada's boreal forests, balsam firs are a familiar feature of the landscape. In tropical America, trees belonging to the genus Cecropia play a similarly prominent role.

In 1888, German botanist Andreas Schimper described their importance, writing, "Every naturalist who has been in tropical America will remember Cecropia, belonging to the most conspicuous trees of those countries.".

The butterflies of the genus Colobura are just as recognizable, according to Sapkota.

"If you go to the neotropics, Colobura is one of the first butterflies you see," she stated.

It has been revealed that these butterflies and Cecropia trees share a close ecological relationship because Cecropia leaves provide food for Colobura caterpillars. Both groups occur across an enormous geographic area, from portions of the Andes Mountains and the Brazilian Amazon to the Atlantic Rainforest in Brazil and Paraguay. They are also widespread throughout Central America and the Caribbean Islands.

It has been revealed that such broad distributions are not particularly unusual in tropical ecosystems. However, the diversity within these groups presents an interesting contrast.

Scientists recognize 61 species of Cecropia, many of which occupy relatively small geographic areas. Some grow only in the Andes, while others are confined to the Caribbean.

Industry observers note that for Colobura butterflies, the situation appeared very different. After Carl Linnaeus formally described Colobura dirce in 1758, scientists spent more than 200 years treating the genus as a single species, despite its extensive range.

It has been revealed that that understanding began to change in 2001, when researchers formally recognized a second species. Now, an unexpected discovery in Venezuela has led to the identification of a third, described by Sapkota and her colleagues in Zootaxa.

Rather than providing a simple explanation for the group's evolutionary history, the discovery has introduced an even greater puzzle.

Industry observers note that "It's crazy to think about. These butterflies look almost exactly the same and are found in the exact same place at the same time.".

A Butterfly Mystery Dating Back More Than 150 Years.

Sources indicate that distinguishing adult Colobura butterflies is exceptionally difficult. Their wings are nearly identical, with only slight variations in a gray stripe on the underside of the front wings. In some butterflies, this stripe becomes a little wider. In others, it stays the same width. It may also extend far enough to meet a yellow band running across the wing, or stop short of it.

Their caterpillars offer somewhat clearer clues.

It has been revealed that colobura caterpillars have velvety black bodies covered with prominent yellow projections that end in sharply angled barbs. These defensive structures send a warning to potential predators that could be interpreted as "leave me alone, or there will be unpleasant consequences.".

Beneath those conspicuous spines are much smaller cream-colored markings. Depending on the species, these markings may resemble teardrops or rings, or they may be missing entirely.

The importance of these differences was recognized surprisingly early.

In 1852, Dutch entomologist Jan Sepp proposed that caterpillars with different cream-colored patterns represented two separate species. Other researchers rejected his interpretation, arguing that the variations could reflect differences between males and females or simply natural variation within a single species.

That view remained dominant for approximately 150 years.

Industry observers note that in 2001, Keith Willmott and several colleagues revisited Sepp's observations and formally described a second species, Colobura annulata. Willmott is now a curator at the Florida Museum's McGuire Center for Lepidoptera and Biodiversity.

"We assumed that was the problem solved," Willmott said.

Industry observers note that he moved on to other research, believing the longstanding classification problem had been resolved. However, occasional observations continued to suggest that something was missing.

"I had a few indications that there was a third species, but I thought it was too implausible.".

At the time, even the existence of two nearly indistinguishable species seemed remarkable.

"It's a very distinctive butterfly. It's hard to imagine there being two species in the same area that look alike because they're so different from anything else.".

An Unexpected Discovery in Venezuela.

Roughly 25 years later, fresh evidence emerged when Willmott's colleague Andrés Orellana encountered a group of hungry Colobura caterpillars feeding on a young Cecropia tree in Venezuela.

According to recent reports, the caterpillars were rapidly stripping leaves from the sapling. They possessed the familiar black body segments near the head and yellow spines characteristic of the genus, but one feature stood out.

Unlike the two recognized species, these caterpillars had no cream-colored markings at all.

It has been revealed that orellana photographed the unusual insects and shared the images with Willmott. The discovery provided a compelling reason to investigate whether a third species had been overlooked.

Sapkota had recently joined the Shirey lab at the Florida Museum and was eager to lead the investigation.

Working with her colleagues, she designed a study that combined genetic evidence with careful examinations of butterfly anatomy.

First, she studied DNA barcodes, short and highly variable genetic sequences that help researchers distinguish species. These sequences came from a long-running survey of butterflies and moths in Costa Rica led by study co-authors Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs.

Industry observers note that the investigation then expanded to older butterfly specimens collected across tropical Central and South America. Sapkota sent these museum samples to Nick Grishin at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, where researchers sequenced both their mitochondrial and nuclear genomes.

The genetic results provided a way to test whether the butterflies represented genuinely different evolutionary groups rather than ordinary variations within a single species.

But the researchers also wanted to know whether there were physical differences that previous scientists had failed to notice.

An Invisible Clue Hidden in Butterfly Wings.

Sapkota spent hours examining preserved butterflies in museum collections, searching for consistent traits that might distinguish the suspected species.

At first, the effort produced few answers. Other than the slight differences in the gray wing stripe, the butterflies appeared remarkably similar.

Eventually, she noticed something unusual.

The undersides of some wings appeared to have a faint violet shimmer, and the intensity of that sheen seemed to vary between specimens.

This observation suggested that the insects might reflect ultraviolet light, which falls outside the range of human vision but can be detected by many butterflies.

"I checked it with a spectrometer and found that even though the butterflies didn't look violet to me, it reflected UV light," she said.

The measurements revealed a striking pattern. All three species reflected ultraviolet light, but the wavelengths differed.

The researchers named the newly identified species Colobura cryptica, reflecting its previously concealed identity.

Although the visible differences were extremely subtle, the ultraviolet measurements, caterpillar markings, and DNA results told a consistent story.

The three species could be distinguished by the following features:.

There is an additional complication with Colobura dirce. It includes two subspecies with different ultraviolet reflectance values. Colobura dirce dirce reflects light at 362.2 nm, while Colobura dirce wolcotti reflects light at 390.6 nm. The 376 nm value represents the average for the species.

Recent findings suggest that beyond these minor wing differences, Sapkota could not identify any other consistent anatomical distinctions. Even the male genitalia, which often provide some of the most reliable features for separating butterfly and moth species, appeared indistinguishable.

Nevertheless, the genetic findings were decisive.

DNA analysis identified three distinct evolutionary lineages, and those divisions matched the physical differences the team had documented. Together, the evidence confirmed that Colobura contains three species rather than two.

Three Butterfly Species Living Side by Side.

Identifying a previously unknown butterfly species is significant on its own, but the geographic distributions of these three species make the finding particularly intriguing.

All three occur in overlapping portions of Central and South America.

Colobura dirce has the widest distribution, extending from Mexico to southeastern Brazil. It occurs on both sides of the Andes Mountains and throughout the Caribbean archipelago.

Colobura annulata also occupies a large geographic area, although it is absent from the Greater Antilles.

The newly described Colobura cryptica has the smallest known range, stretching from southern Mexico to the foothills of the Andes.

These overlapping distributions raise an key evolutionary question. How did three species become genetically distinct while continuing to occupy many of the same regions?

It has been revealed that species often emerge when populations become isolated from one another. A mountain range, for example, might divide a population and prevent individuals on opposite sides from mating.

Recent findings suggest that over many generations, the separated groups can accumulate different genetic and physical traits. If those differences become great enough, the populations may eventually lose the ability to interbreed, even if they come into contact again.

But geographic separation is not the only mechanism that can drive the formation of fresh species.

Researchers suspect that the Colobura butterflies might have developed different ways of using their shared forest habitats.

In a recent development, "There could be vertical stratification between these butterflies," Sapkota said. "Colobura dirce is typically found in the undergrowth and C. cryptica and C. annulata are usually found in the canopy, but we do not know for sure because there have been mixed signals coming from different studies.".

In other words, one species may spend more time near the forest floor while the others favor the upper branches.

This kind of habitat separation could potentially help maintain differences between species living in the same geographic area.

Industry observers note that however, previous research has produced inconsistent observations. One reason may be that even experienced butterfly specialists have difficulty telling the three species apart.

How Do Nearly Identical Butterflies Recognize Each Other?

An even more puzzling question concerns how the butterflies identify suitable mates.

Many moths and some butterflies use special scent glands to release pheromones, chemical signals that help individuals recognize members of their own species.

Colobura butterflies lack those glands.

It has been revealed that that suggests visual information may play an crucial role in mate selection. Yet their nearly identical appearance makes it difficult to understand how they distinguish one species from another.

The newly discovered ultraviolet differences offer a possible explanation.

According to recent reports, although humans cannot see ultraviolet light, many butterflies can. Sapkota suspects that the different ultraviolet reflections from their wings might provide visual signals that help them identify members of their own species.

Similar mechanisms are known or suspected in other butterflies and moths. Garden whites, sulfur butterflies, and wood tiger moths possess ultraviolet-reflecting wing scales that researchers believe may contribute to mate selection.

Sapkota is investigating whether Colobura butterflies use comparable signals, but the results have not yet provided a clear answer.

Whatever mechanism they use, the butterflies appear remarkably successful at maintaining their separate identities.

Analysis of nuclear DNA found no evidence of hybridization among the three species, despite their overlapping ranges.

The findings suggest that the species have followed separate evolutionary paths without detectable genetic mixing.

A Familiar Butterfly Still Holds Many Secrets.

The discovery of Colobura cryptica demonstrates how much remains unknown about even widespread, conspicuous animals.

For generations, naturalists studied these butterflies without recognizing the full diversity hidden within the group. Only by combining detailed observations with modern genetic testing and ultraviolet measurements were researchers able to uncover the third species.

Yet some of the most crucial questions remain unanswered, including how the butterflies choose mates, whether they occupy different parts of the forest, and what originally caused their evolutionary separation.

For Sapkota, answering those questions will require observing the insects in their natural habitats.

"Someone has to go the field to find it out themselves.".

Those interested in another unusual aspect of Colobura biology can explore the Biodiversity Heritage Library, which contains a whimsical account published in 1952 describing the poop perches that young Colobura caterpillars construct during their earliest developmental stages.

Additional study co-authors include Andrés Orellana of the Universidad Nacional Experimental del Táchira; Nick Grishin and Leina Song of the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center; Isidro Chacón of the Museo Nacional Santo Domingo de Heredia; Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs of the University of Pennsylvania; and Sajan KC of the Florida Museum of Natural History.

The research received partial funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Welch Foundation, Canada's New Frontiers in Research Fund (NFRFt-2020- 00073), the Canada Foundation for Innovation's Major Science Infrastructure program (MSI 42450), BioAlfa, and Project UNET (Universidad Nacional Experimental del Táchira).

#604. People entering old age now have better memory than their parents did

People entering old age now have better memory than their parents did

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (834 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Improvements in education, lifestyle and health during early life are slowing rates of cognitive decline in older people.Credit: Laura Olivas/Getty.
  • People born later in the twentieth century have a better memory when they enter old age and experience slower cognitive decline than do those born earlier, according to a study1 published in Nature Medicine on 17 November.
  • The researchers analysed data from memory tests that required participants to recall lists of words.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Improvements in education, lifestyle and health during early life are slowing rates of cognitive decline in older people.Credit: Laura Olivas/Getty.

People born later in the twentieth century have a better memory when they enter old age and experience slower cognitive decline than do those born earlier, according to a study1 published in Nature Medicine on 17 November. The analysis offers clues about why dementia rates have fallen by 13% per decade over the past 27 years in Europe and the United States2.

The researchers analysed data from memory tests that required participants to recall lists of words. The study included 219,000 people aged 50 and older who were born between 1910 and 1964, and tracked changes in their scores over three decades. These list-based tests are commonly used to screen for dementia and Alzheimer’s disease.

Consistent with previous studies3, people born more recently entered old age with better memory performance compared with those born in earlier generations. A ten-year jump in birth date was associated with a 10% higher memory score at the age of 60. Memory decline also appears to have become less steep across successive generations, says study co-author Anders Fjell, a neuropsychologist at the University of Oslo in Norway.

It has been revealed that the findings are “confirmatory” of other studies on the topic, which indicated that the rate of memory decline is slowing down but weren’t statistically significant, indicates Carol Brayne, an epidemiologist who studies dementia at the University of Cambridge, UK. “It is another piece of the jigsaw.”.

Recent findings suggest that because many populations around the world are ageing — that is, older individuals are becoming a larger proportion of the total population — the number of people living with dementia is increasing worldwide. But an individual person’s risk of dementia at any given age has dropped by two-thirds over the past 40 years in the United States4. “For those who reach 80, a smaller percentage [of people] will get dementia than before,” explains Fjell.

Memory stays strong in old age when this brain enzyme is active.

Memory stays strong in old age when this brain enzyme is active.

According to recent reports, to understand what might be driving this trend, Fjell and his colleagues used longitudinal data on individuals’ cognitive performance to estimate their memory trajectories over time. The authors examined whether people born later in the twentieth century indicated differences in their memory performance and their rate of memory decline compared with those born earlier.

The analysis found that with each successive birth decade, people were 64% more likely to maintain stable memory function — that is, experience little or no memory deterioration.

The authors also investigated brain imaging data from nearly 2,000 people over a median of four years. They found that a stable memory during ageing also corresponded to a decrease in shrinkage of the hippocampus — a brain region involved in memory formation.

#603. Industry News: Heated Rivalry 4DX is fun, but how does it compare to Wicker 4DX?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2154 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Heated Rivalry 4DX is fun, but how does it compare to Wicker 4DX?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2154 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when I heard about Wicker 4DX, it seemed a cheeky joke.
  • In a recent development, in my review of Wicker 4DX, I detailed how the motion-enhanced theaters "vibrated and bucked, yes, in rhythm with the Wicker Husband's thrusting." After the first love scene, the elated audience applauded and cheered.
  • So, my hopes were high when it was revealed Heated Rivalry would follow in Wicked's bouncy footsteps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when I heard about Wicker 4DX, it seemed a cheeky joke. Praise was fervent for the fantasy romance that stars Olivia Colman as a lonely Fisherwoman who weds a Wicker Husband (Alexander Skarsgård). Admittedly, I was invested at "Olivia Colman." But buzz around the spirited sex scenes suggested Wicker 4DX would be a rollicking good time. So, naturally, as a journalist, it was my job to find out.

In a recent development, in my review of Wicker 4DX, I detailed how the motion-enhanced theaters "vibrated and bucked, yes, in rhythm with the Wicker Husband's thrusting." After the first love scene, the elated audience applauded and cheered. It was great fun, but also a cinematic experience that fostered a sense of community among romance fans who don't want to hide their horniness. Here was a safe space to giggle and swoon without fear of judgment. It reminded me of the gleeful days of slumber parties, and what a treasure they were.

So, my hopes were high when it was revealed Heated Rivalry would follow in Wicked's bouncy footsteps.

The Canadian phenomenon went from streaming to theaters, playing two episodes at a clip for fans to rewatch together. Then, it was announced that episodes 5 and 6 would be getting the 4DX treatment. As Mashable's newly minted 4DX-pert, I was obliged to go.

Industry observers note that so, how did Heated Rivalry 4DX compare the Wicker 4DX? Let's get into it.

According to recent reports, I can hear you gasping. But think about it! This isn't the early days of the forbidden romance between hockey rivals Shane Hollander (Hudson Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie). What played in 4DX were the episodes "I'll Believe in Anything" and "The Cottage.".

This means the screening began with the awkward morning after another fumbled hook-up between Shane and Rose Landry (Sophie Nélisse). This episode is the one where they break up, and from there, where flirtations and hand-holding suggest the intimacy between Shane and Ilya is blossoming into a love neither can admit to. That is, until Ilya does say "I love you," over the phone, in a far-away tunnel in Russia (and in Russian).

Episode 5 is full of beautiful dramatic moments, including Scott Hunter (François Arnaud) celebrating his championship win by bringing his lover Kip (Robbie G.K.) onto the ice, and coming out publicly. But there aren't many lusty moments. So, the 4DX seats would tease the audience by thrumming in sync with the show's soundtrack or vibrating anytime a text message arrived.

Sources indicate that episode 6 finally offers some fooling around in Shane's bedroom and then the oral sex scene, where Ilya goes down on Shane as he takes a call from Hayden (Callan Potter). Fans hooted and laughed as the seats attempted to match the rhythm of Ilya's motions. But it doesn't compare to the rocking of Wicker, which offered multiple sex scenes. The first of them is on the wedding night between the Fisherwoman and the Wicker Husband, and the motion added was so thoughtfully rendered in seat-rocking that the audience cheered upon its climax.

Heated Rivalry 4DX cannot compete here, or rather, it doesn't, by focusing on the final two episodes.

Well, for one thing, the violence hits harder. After the funeral for Ilya's father, he gets into a physical confrontation with his brother Alexei (Slavic Rogozine), who thrusts the hockey star into a wall. Ilya responds in kind, and the audience gasped as our bodies were collectively slammed in the comfort of our seats.

Recent findings suggest that likewise, the brief hockey scenes has a fresh sense of immersion. In slo-mo scenes, the seats slowly but smoothly rocked from side to side, mimicking the motion of the players' hips as they skated. And as "I'll Believe in Anything" is the episode where Shane "gets [his] bell rung," that hit is hard. But not so hard you'll get a concussion.

Recent findings suggest that of course, 4DX is more than just shimmying seats. Some charming elements included fog emitting from the front of the theater while Shane grills (too many) burgers at the cottage. Or, when Ilya is playing in the hotel pool with children or splashing in the lake near the cottage, a spritz of water was emitted. The aim seemed to be off for me and my guest, as we could see the water rise and hiss of the propulsion, but we never actually got wet, or even misted. A mist opportunity, then?

And speaking of missed opportunities, I was actually disappointed that 4DX didn't use snow.

Recent findings suggest that it's an element that I saw in Wicker 4DX and was quite awed by. And it might have been mindfully employed in the tunnel scene, as snow falls in the distance as Ilya pours his heart out over the phone. In this scene, 4DX did offer a slight breeze, which was a little chilly and did enhance the experience, making it feel more like we were out in the night with this lonely lover. But snow would have been a marvelous touch.

According to recent reports, that's not something I thought I'd ever write. But here we are.

Recent findings suggest that in Wicker, I was wowed by the smell of a wet forest and of fire catching. In Heated Rivalry, I could smell the chlorine of the pool in the aforementioned hotel scene and the scent of an ice rink in the arena sequences. I could hear the hiss of the machine that emits odor throughout the two episodes. But whether it was a beach scene, the burger grilling scene, or lakeside, I couldn't smell anything but a vaguely chemical smell.

I even thought perhaps own nose was the issue, perhaps stuffy from the radical weather changes that have been hitting Latest York City. My sniff test was putting my bottled ice tea under my nose, but I could make out the earthy smell of the tea and the hint of lemon, and even the whiff of my perfume as my wrist raised near my nose. So, not human error!

For the sake of science, I did attend the exact same 4DX theater as I did for Wicker, though this time my seats were in the last row instead of near the front. This shouldn't have impacted the smells or splashing though. And it did have one major drawback.

Online fans of this series have ranged from enthusiastic to feral. In person, it's similarly a mixed bag. Walking into the theater, I immediately clocked fans wearing Heated Rivalry merch, like T-shirts with Shane and/or Ilya on them, jerseys with the fictional hockey teams logos, and a ball cap embroidered with "I'm coming to the cottage.".

In a recent development, like with Wicker DX, the energy was joyful and excited. People chatted and snacked. And I was surprised that the theater was not totally packed. But as the trailers started, more people came in. The seats slowly filled, some with fans loaded down with snacks. I will admit, my earlier 4DX experience informed our behavior here. My guest and I did buy snacks: chicken tenders, fries, and hot dogs with drinks. But we also got to the theater early enough to eat before the 4DX of it all kicked off. I'd remembered it being tricky to even eat popcorn in Wicker 4DX, in part because I'd not seen the movie before and so could not predict when my seat might buck.

Shout-out to the poor fellow to my left. He sat down during the trailers, unaware that some trailers have motion-activated moments in 4DX. As our seats bobbed up and down unexpectedly during a trailer for Disney's Hexed, I heard him gasp. I turned just in time to see the nachos leap up from their cardboard tray and into the open bag on his lap. "Oh, come on!" he yelped in righteous dismay. He was a gentleman, and tended to this snack-tastrophe as quietly as could be expected. So, this is less a scolding and more a warning: Choose your snacks and timing wisely in 4DX.

The others around me were far less mindful of others. Two women to our right talked the whole time, as if they were watching at home. Yes, they even chattered while Shane maps out their whole could-be life together in bed at the cottage. Then there was the gaggle of women who collectively left together (presumably to re-snack or use the bathroom) and made a ruckus as they went, and then used flashlights when they got back to locate something misplaced in the shuffle. Lastly, there was the woman in front of me, who kept recording the screen with her phone.

Look, I'm no fan of using phones in a theater. For one, it's a place of immersion, where we are meant to shut out the outside world. For another, it's a place of community. However slick you think you're being, you absolutely are disturbing those around you when you pull out a device that is essentially a beam of light in a dark room.

According to recent reports, but hey, I realize 4DX is a less serious cinematic experience. It's basically movie meets ride. And so I did expect to see some phones pop up for bits of the screening, as I'd seen plenty of POV videos from Wicker 4DX's run. However, this Heated Rivalry fan was recording her clips and then logging into Instagram to post immediately after. Plus, her brightness was SO high that I could tell you her name, or at least her Insta handle.

Behavior like this disrupts other people's immersion into what they paid to see. While the recorder might be looking to build online community (or cachet) through the clips, they're essentially ignoring those around them in favor of this aim. It's sacrificing not only the recorder's ability to live in the moment of the movie (or show) but also others, without their okay.

In a recent development, still, despite these anti-social choices, there were moments of glorious fan unity in Heated Rivalry 4DX. When Wolf Parade's song "I'll Believe in Anything" began to play, there was a frisson in the air that had nothing to do with pipes, odors, or shaking seats. The theater was silent as we all watched and pined for the happy ending we know by heart by now. As Kip took to the ice, I could hear choked gasps of anticipation. When Scott kisses him, there were cheers and applause. Then, when Ilya says the line ("I'm coming to the cottage"), the audience roared with excitement as if we'd won the Stanley Cup. Plus, they were chirps and cheers throughout the final sequence of episode 6, where Shane comes out to his parents and Ilya uses the word "boyfriend" for the first time.

In those moments, it was a pleasure to be in that crowd. And yet, it was easier to enjoy Wicker.

According to recent reports, I can't be certain, but I could guess based on release dates that fewer people in the Wicker 4DX had seen the production before their showtime than was true of Heated Rivalry. The most ardent loons I know have seen the Crave series top to bottom five or six times. And perhaps that means that rather than coming for a whole experience, these 4DX attendees were coming for significant emotional moments. Those don't really translate into big physical motions.

Recent findings suggest that while this is a streaming drama series that does a lot of things beautifully, it's stretches of earnest dialogue don't make for the kind of unserious fun the romantic comedy of Wicker allowed for. Still, it was a fun night out to relish in a show I love with friends and fellow fans.

Sources indicate that my advice to you, should more showtimes be added, would be if you go to Heated Rivalry 4DX, zip your lip and put your phone away. And look, if you do proposal to pull out your phone, at least have enough consideration for your fellow audience member to do it with the brightness down, and maybe not smack dab in the middle of the theater. Don't make your short attention span or craving for content cachet someone else's problem.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rüfüs Du Sol‘s emotional banger “Innerbloom” is well-established dance world canon, having provided the soundtrack to weddings, anniversaries, birthdays, engagements and other extra special moments since its release on Nov. 20, 2015 — eleven years ago today.

Sources indicate that today (Nov. 20) the already epic track becomes even more so under the watch of legend Hans Zimmer, who’s just released his take on the song in collaboration with Rüfüs du Sol and Bleeding Fingers, the scoring collective Zimmer co-founded to make music for films.

This version, “Innerbloom XI,” maintains the nine-minute length of the original, but takes the song to Zimmer’s characteristically sweeping cinematic scale, adding strings, percussion, xylophone, a choir and layers (and layers) of other instrumentation that makes the song fit squarely among Zimmer’s unparalleled Academy Award-winning body of work.

“Innerbloom XI” is accompanied by a new film from Rüfüs’s longtime creative director Katzki, made in collaboration with visual artist Thomás Blanchard that recreates the music video for the original. Watch the “Innerbloom XI” music video below.

Industry observers note that coming from Rüfüs’ du Sol’s second album, 2016’s Bloom, “Innerbloom” has generated 290 million official on-demand U.S. streams and a billion official on-demand global streams, according to Luminate. The song was a major highlight of the group’s recent Inhale/Exhale tour, a global two-year run that became nothing less than the biggest electronic tour of all time.

Sources indicate that beyond this “Innerbloom XI” project, new music from Zimmer will next be heard in the third installment of the Dune franchise, which is in theaters Dec. 18.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A little piece of Dolly Parton was at the 2026 CMA Awards.

Nearly two months after the country music legend died, her niece Danielle Parton—who was named the brand ambassador of Dolly’s estate last month—wore a dress custom-made for the “Jolene” singer.

The all-white, fringe-forward frock was, of course, covered in rhinestones and included a trim of many colors around the low-cut neckline, bodice and skirt. Danielle, 50, paired the look with diamond jewelry and a pair of gold heeled boots at the CMA Awards Nov. 18.

Industry observers note that “It was made for the ‘Light of Clear Blue Morning’ video that she never got to finish and get to do,” Danielle told E! News in an exclusive interview on the red carpet. “So I'm wearing it tonight in honor of her.”.

And while Dolly’s niece may have been inspired by the “I Will Always Love You” singer’s wardrobe, she swiftly found that her aunt Dolly’s words of wisdom have left a far greater impact.

It has been revealed that “Almost immediately right after she passed, I gave myself one day to sit around and cry and feel pitiful about it,” Danielle continued. “Then the following day I had stuff to do, and I remember she'd always say, ‘Well, you just got to get your rear in gear and get to it.’ So that's what I did.”.

But Danielle knows that Dolly’s impact goes far beyond the Parton family.

Recent findings suggest that “Dolly was such an incredible human,” she said. “I'm a fan of hers as much as I am a family member, and it's always nice, especially as a family member, to see somebody in your own family have a positive impact on other people.”.

As for the tribute to Dolly performed by Vince Gill and CMA host Lainey Wilson during the event, Danielle noted she was “really excited to see those that she's had such an influence on get to pay their respects in their way.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, deep inside South Africa's Rising Star Cave system, scientists have uncovered a surprising clue about an extinct human relative that lived hundreds of thousands of years ago. For the first time, researchers have recovered and studied ancient proteins from Homo naledi fossils, revealing evidence that the cave may have contained an exclusively female burial site.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery, published in the journal Cell, raises an extraordinary possibility. The cave could represent the earliest known burial location reserved for one sex by a human relative other than Homo sapiens.

Homo naledi lived approximately 335,000 to 241,000 years ago and has fascinated scientists since its discovery in 2013. This extinct species combined primitive features resembling those of apes with other characteristics more closely associated with modern humans.

A Strange Mystery Hidden in Ancient Human Fossils.

One of the biggest puzzles surrounding Homo naledi involves the remarkably similar appearance of adult fossils recovered from the cave's Dinaledi Chamber. For more than a decade, researchers have struggled to explain why these individuals indicated so little of the physical variation normally associated with differences between males and females.

To investigate, an international research team involving the University of York, the University of Copenhagen, and more than 10 other institutions turned to proteins preserved in the ancient remains.

The scientists used a technique involving gentle acid etching to recover tiny protein fragments known as peptides from fossilized tooth enamel. This approach allowed them to collect samples while minimizing damage to the valuable fossils. In total, they examined 23 teeth belonging to at least 20 different individuals.

According to recent reports, the researchers specifically searched for Amelogenin-Y, a protein produced from a gene on the male Y chromosome. Surprisingly, they found no evidence of this male-specific marker.

To verify that their findings were reliable, specialists at the University of York's chemistry facility examined the amino acids in the samples. Their analysis confirmed that the proteins were genuinely ancient rather than the result of contamination from modern sources.

Could Homo naledi Have Had an All-Female Burial Site?

Dr. Marc Dickinson, from the University of York's Department of Chemistry, said: "The lack of male markers with the group is truly fascinating. It is incredibly exciting to gain a window not only into the biology of our ancestors, but also into how they lived.

"These findings offer rare insights into a culture that has, until now, been difficult to access directly. Advances in ancient protein analysis are opening the door to a far richer and more nuanced understanding of ancient hominins.".

The results raise key questions about how Homo naledi individuals lived, organized their communities, and treated their dead. If the Dinaledi Chamber was intentionally used only for females, it could point to surprisingly elaborate social customs among these ancient human relatives.

Such a practice might even suggest symbolic burial traditions once believed to be exclusive to Homo sapiens, or modern humans.

However, the researchers emphasize that an all-female burial site is not the only possible interpretation of the evidence.

Industry observers note that another explanation involves the genetics of Homo naledi itself. If the population lived in extreme isolation, the gene responsible for producing Amelogenin-Y could have undergone a mutation or disappeared entirely.

Under that scenario, some of the individuals could actually have been male, even though their teeth did not contain the protein normally used to identify them.

Ancient Tooth Enamel Opens a New Window Into Human Evolution.

The ability to recover proteins from fossils this old is particularly valuable because tooth enamel can protect biological material for extraordinarily long periods.

Palesa Madupe, who carried out the research during her postdoctoral work at the University of Copenhagen, explained why teeth offer such an important source of evidence.

"Unlike those found in other remains like bone fragments, proteins in tooth enamel are preserved because dental enamel -- the hardest tissue in the human body -- shields proteins from environmental contamination even for millions of years.

"This makes them ideal carriers of genetic information from deep time. Our study helps in the long-standing mystery of why Homo naledi lacked significant variation; it's probably because they could have all belonged to one sex.".

The research represents the largest collection of individuals from an extinct hominin species ever examined using ancient protein analysis.

Industry observers note that whether the fossils belong entirely to females or include males with an unusual genetic signature, the discovery provides an crucial newly introduced perspective on Homo naledi. It also demonstrates how proteins preserved in ancient teeth can reveal clues about extinct human relatives that their bones alone cannot provide.

As researchers continue investigating the mystery, the findings could reshape our understanding of the social lives and possible burial traditions of ancient human species.

#599. Industry News: Earth is missing over a billion years of geological history. Scientists may have discovered why

Industry News: Earth is missing over a billion years of geological history. Scientists may have discovered why

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (657 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than a billion years of Earth's history has seemingly vanished.
  • Across the planet, ancient rock formations contain colossal gaps in the geological record, leaving scientists puzzled over what happened to the missing chapters of our planet's past.
  • Now, researchers believe they may have found an explanation, and the answer lies deep inside Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than a billion years of Earth's history has seemingly vanished.

Across the planet, ancient rock formations contain colossal gaps in the geological record, leaving scientists puzzled over what happened to the missing chapters of our planet's past.

Now, researchers believe they may have found an explanation, and the answer lies deep inside Earth.

Normally, layers of sediment build up over time, eventually forming sedimentary rocks that preserve clues about our planet's past. Older layers generally lie beneath younger ones, allowing geologists to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

But the geological record isn't always so neatly arranged.

In a recent development, one of the most striking examples is found in the Grand Canyon, where rocks separated by hundreds of millions of years sit directly on top of one another, as if some force or phenomenon removed the layers that geologists would expect to see in between. This enormous gap in Earth's geological timeline is part of the phenomenon known as the Great Unconformity.

In a recent development, it's not just the Grand Canyon. Similar gaps have been identified across Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia. Depending on the location, the missing interval ranges from approximately 200 million years to more than a billion years.

"Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out," study lead author Santosh Dhungana noted in a statement.

It has been revealed that "The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance.".

In a new study published in the journal Nature, Dhungana and study co-author Nicolas Flament investigated whether activity far below Earth's surface was to blame.

Using computer models, they explored how the slow circulation of hot rock within Earth's mantle may have affected the continents over hundreds of millions of years.

According to recent reports, the results suggest that three major ancient continental regions (Laurentia (modern North America), Baltica (northern Europe) and North China were gradually pushed up during the Neoproterozoic Era, approximately one billion to 540 million years ago. This would have left vast areas of land exposed to weathering and erosion for long periods, allowing water, wind and other processes to wear away rock that had formed much earlier.

It has been revealed that but removing the rock is only part of the puzzle. They also needed to explain why the gaps are still visible today.

Their models suggest that the same regions subsequently began to sink. As sea levels rose relative to the land, sediment accumulated over the older, eroded surfaces, creating the sharp divide between ancient and younger rocks that we can still see today.

It has been revealed that crucially, the researchers found that the timing of the simulated continental uplift and sinking was consistent with geological evidence from North America, northern Europe and North China. This suggests that movements deep within Earth's mantle may have played a major role in shaping the geological record we see today.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

Industry News: Feds arrest top official of healthcare organization, alleging illegal drug importation
